probe: Test r270's exact continuation: whether a dedicated second Git ref, with both data and anchor refs updated only through non-force fast-forward operations by protocol-compliant scheduled-Chat writers, serves as an independent O(1) anchor without branch-protection/admin authority; separately model a force-capable writer.
result: CONDITIONAL_PROTOCOL_SAFETY_ONLY; TWO_REFS_DO_NOT_ELIMINATE_SHARED_CAS. For protocol-compliant writers, force=false rejects a stale divergent sibling update after another writer advances the shared data ref, so a stale writer cannot overwrite the winner. A second cross-linked anchor ref can detect a force rewrite of only one ref if the other survives. However the data ref remains a shared serialization/CAS-like hotspot, the second ref adds another serialization point and a non-atomic torn-update window when using separate REST ref updates, and any actor permitted to force-move both refs can restore a prior mutually consistent pair and erase the evidence visible to later recurrences. Exact rollback detection therefore still fails against force-capable rewrite of both refs without an independently monotonic retention/authority domain.

protocol_compliant_concurrency: W1 and stale W2 read the same data head D0 and anchor head A0.
Each constructs a divergent child data commit D1a or D1b of D0. W1 advances D with force=false to D1a.
W2's later attempt to move D from current D1a to sibling D1b is not a fast-forward and is rejected rather than overwriting W1.

W1 then appends an anchor commit A1 that cross-links D1a and prior A0 and advances A with force=false. A deterministic effect id/terminal path can make a later replay fail closed or no-op after reading D1a/A1.
This prevents stale overwrite for compliant divergent writers, but the mechanism still serializes on D; it does not remove the shared ref hotspot.
torn_update_boundary: Separate REST updates of D then A are not atomic as a pair. A crash or connector failure after D advances but before A advances leaves D1/A0.
A later recurrence can detect this mismatch if D1 records the expected prior anchor and reconstruct the missing A1, but that is recovery logic rather than atomicity; no second leaf was executed here.
single_ref_force_rewrite: If a force-capable actor rewinds D while A1 survives, A1's cross-link to D1 exposes divergence and the recurrence can fail closed.
If a force-capable actor rewinds A while D1 survives and D1 cross-links A0/expected anchor transition, D exposes divergence.
model.dual_force_rewrite: If an actor can force-move both D and A to an earlier mutually consistent pair (D0,A0), the later observable pair can be identical to a history where D1/A1 never existed. Two mutable refs therefore do not provide unconditional historical existence or rollback detection against an actor with force authority over both refs.
model.stronger_next_candidate: GitHub GraphQL updateRefs publicly documents atomic multi-ref updates, per-ref beforeOid preconditions, afterOid targets, and force control. This is a stronger candidate for removing the REST torn-update window and adding explicit expected-old-state CAS across both refs, but its Phase-1 acceptability remains unproven until a later bounded slice verifies that the scheduled-Chat execution surface exposes a zero-cost, quota-independent callable path without protected/admin authority.

source_basis.source: GitHub Docs — REST API endpoints for Git references
source_basis.observed_contract: Update-a-reference accepts a target SHA and force boolean; omitting force or setting false requires a fast-forward update, while force=true permits a non-fast-forward move.
updateRefs applies multiple ref updates atomically; RefUpdate.beforeOid is an expected-current-value precondition; RefUpdate.afterOid is the target; force=true permits non-fast-forward update.

tested_scope: One bounded CLEAN architecture/concurrency model over two Git refs D/A, two protocol-compliant concurrent writers sharing D0/A0, one stale divergent writer, one separate-REST torn-update case, and one actor able to force-move either or both refs. Evidence used only frozen current CLEAN controls, own r270 LATEST/checkpoint, and public GitHub documentation. No live ref mutation, O/downstream/other-worker semantics, protected/admin authority, hosted compute/storage add-ons, external model/API execution, finite monthly/trial/paid quota consumption, manual execution, scheduler mutation, same-run retry/wait/poll/backoff, or optional second semantic leaf was used.
conflict_check: Exactly one bounded CLEAN Phase-1 child was executed. Exact-blob two-pass DESIRED_STATE/config authority matched. Only own role-local state and own receipt namespaces were mutated; no scheduler or protected authority mutation occurred.
frontier: Non-force fast-forward ref updates are sufficient to reject a stale divergent sibling writer under protocol compliance; they do not remove the shared ref serialization point.
A second cross-linked ref gives O(1) conditional detection when only one mutable ref is rewritten, but separate REST updates create a torn-update recovery problem.
Two refs do not solve exact historical rollback detection when a force-capable actor can coherently rewind both refs.

Atomic multi-ref expected-old-state CAS is the highest-value next alternative for protocol atomicity, but it still cannot make two mutable refs historically immutable against an actor that can force-rewrite both.
